1. Aim

To develop and test RESTful APIs using Node.js and Express.js and understand HTTP methods, request and response handling, routing, status codes, and API testing using Postman for the BiteOrder Restaurant Ordering System.

2. Problem Statement

Develop a RESTful API for an online restaurant ordering and management system (BiteOrder) using Node.js and Express.js. The API allows users and frontend clients to perform complete CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations on restaurant menu items and customer order records. The developed APIs are thoroughly tested using Postman to verify their functionality, request headers, route parameters, JSON request bodies, and corresponding HTTP status codes.

The application demonstrates the following core Full Stack concepts:

  • Understanding REST Architecture principles (Client-Server, Statelessness, Uniform Interface).
  • Creating an asynchronous backend server using Node.js and Express.js.
  • Configuring essential middleware: express.json() and Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS).
  • Defining modular API routes and organizing controllers according to separation of concerns.
  • Implementing complete CRUD operations on food dishes and customer orders.
  • Utilizing HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE.
  • Extracting route parameters (req.params), query strings (req.query), and request bodies (req.body).
  • Sending standardized HTTP status codes (200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error).
  • Exporting and automating test requests using Postman Collections.
  • Integrating the backend API with a React frontend to dynamically fetch and display live menu items.

3. Theory Questions & Answers

Q1. What is an API?
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a structured computing interface that defines interactions between multiple software intermediaries. It specifies the kinds of calls or requests that can be made, how to make them, the data formats that should be used, and the conventions to adhere to. In web development, a Web API enables communication between client applications (e.g., React frontend) and backend web servers over HTTP/HTTPS, abstracting business logic and database access while exposing standardized endpoints for data exchange.
Q2. What is a RESTful API?
A RESTful API is a web service application interface that conforms to the architectural constraints of REST (Representational State Transfer), introduced by Roy Fielding in 2000. RESTful systems treat all data entities as identifiable resources (e.g., /api/menu, /api/orders), where each resource is accessed via a unique Uniform Resource Identifier (URI). Clients interact with these resources using standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to transfer representations of the resources, typically encoded in JSON.
Q3. What are the main principles of REST architecture?
REST is governed by six fundamental architectural constraints:
  1. Client-Server Architecture: Clear separation of concerns between user interface (client) and data storage/logic (server).
  2. Statelessness: Every HTTP request must contain all context necessary to understand and fulfill it; the server retains no client session context between requests.
  3. Cacheability: Responses must explicitly define whether they are cacheable to optimize network efficiency.
  4. Uniform Interface: Standardized interaction across all resources via unique URIs, resource representation via JSON, and self-descriptive headers.
  5. Layered System: Clients interact with endpoints transparently regardless of intermediaries (proxies, load balancers, gateways).
  6. Code-on-Demand (Optional): Servers may optionally deliver executable code (e.g., client-side scripts) to extend client capabilities.
Q4. What are HTTP methods? Explain GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE.
HTTP methods (verbs) designate the intended operation on a resource:
Method CRUD Operation Safe? Idempotent? Typical Status Codes Purpose in BiteOrder
GET Read Yes Yes 200 OK, 404 Not Found Retrieves menu items or orders without modifying server state.
POST Create No No 201 Created, 400 Bad Request Submits JSON body to create a new dish or place a customer order.
PUT Update No Yes 200 OK, 400 Bad Request Updates an existing dish or order status by URI ID.
DELETE Delete No Yes 200 OK, 404 Not Found Removes a dish or cancels an active order by ID.
Q5. What is the purpose of Express.js in backend development?
Express.js is a minimal, unopinionated web framework for Node.js. While native Node.js provides a low-level http module, building robust web APIs with raw Node requires verbose boilerplate for route parsing, JSON decoding, status header management, and error handling. Express streamlines backend development by offering modular routing (app.get(), express.Router()), a composable middleware pipeline, convenient helpers (res.json(), res.status()), and centralized error-handling.
Q6. What is routing in Express.js?
Routing defines how an application responds to a client request to a particular endpoint, determined by the URI path (e.g., /api/menu) and the HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.). Express facilitates modular routing using express.Router(), allowing route definitions to be organized into dedicated files (e.g., menuRoutes.js) and mounted onto a root prefix (app.use('/api', menuRoutes)).
Q7. What is the purpose of req and res in Express.js?
  • req (Request Object): Represents the incoming HTTP request. Encapsulates query strings (req.query), route parameters (req.params), parsed JSON body data (req.body), and HTTP headers (req.headers).
  • res (Response Object): Represents the outgoing HTTP response. Provides chained methods to set status codes (res.status(200)), configure headers, and return JSON data (res.json()) to the client.
Q8. What is the purpose of req.params and req.body?
Feature req.params req.body
Definition Parameters extracted from the URL path. Data sent in the HTTP request payload.
Configuration Defined via colon syntax in route (/api/menu/:id). Requires body parser (app.use(express.json())).
Typical Verbs GET, PUT, DELETE (identifying specific entities). POST, PUT (transmitting entity attributes).
Data Type Strings by default (e.g., "1"). Parsed JavaScript objects and arrays.
Q9. What is JSON, and why is it commonly used in APIs?
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight, human-readable data-interchange format. It is universally used in RESTful APIs because it is language-independent, compact (much lower network overhead than XML), parsed natively in web browsers via JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify(), and maps directly to native JavaScript objects and arrays.
Q10. What are HTTP status codes? Explain 200, 201, 400, 404, and 500.
Standard 3-digit numerical codes returned by a web server indicating the result of an HTTP request:
  • 200 OK: Standard success code for successful queries (GET) or updates (PUT/DELETE).
  • 201 Created: The request succeeded and resulted in the creation of a new resource (POST).
  • 400 Bad Request: Client error due to missing required fields or malformed data syntax.
  • 404 Not Found: The requested resource URI does not exist on the server.
  • 500 Internal Server Error: The server encountered an unhandled exception or internal error.
Q11. What is Postman, and why is it used for API testing?
Postman is a specialized API platform for constructing, sending, and testing HTTP requests. While web browsers only send GET requests from their address bar, Postman allows developers to execute all HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), configure headers and request bodies, inspect status codes and latency, and group requests into automated, exportable collections.
Q12. What is the purpose of the request body and headers in Postman?
  • Headers: Transmit request metadata such as Content-Type: application/json (instructing Express to decode JSON via middleware) and Accept: application/json.
  • Request Body: The actual JSON payload transmitted to create or update resources on the server (configured under Body → raw → JSON).
Q13. What is CRUD, and how is it implemented using RESTful APIs?
CRUD represents Create, Read, Update, and Delete. In RESTful web services, CRUD maps to HTTP methods:
  • Create: POST /api/menu → Creates a new dish (Returns 201 Created).
  • Read: GET /api/menu (all) and GET /api/menu/:id (single) → Returns 200 OK.
  • Update: PUT /api/menu/:id → Modifies an existing dish by ID (Returns 200 OK).
  • Delete: DELETE /api/menu/:id → Removes a dish by ID (Returns 200 OK).
Q14. What is middleware in Express.js?
Middleware functions have access to the request object (req), response object (res), and the next() function. Middleware can execute code, modify request and response objects, terminate the request-response cycle (e.g., returning a 400 error on validation failure), or call next() to pass control to the next handler in the stack.

4. Source Code Implementation

4.1 Creating the Express Server with CORS & Middleware (server/server.js)

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
const menuRoutes = require('./routes/menuRoutes');

// 1. CORS Middleware (Enables cross-origin requests from React client)
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*');
  res.header('Access-Control-Allow-Methods', 'GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS');
  res.header('Access-Control-Allow-Headers', 'Origin, X-Requested-With, Content-Type, Accept');
  if (req.method === 'OPTIONS') return res.sendStatus(200);
  next();
});

// 2. Built-in JSON Body Parser Middleware
app.use(express.json());

// 3. Custom Request Logger Middleware
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  console.log(`[${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}] ${req.method} ${req.url}`);
  next();
});

// 4. Mount API Routes on /api prefix
app.use('/api', menuRoutes);

// 5. 404 Route Not Found Fallback Handler
app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).json({ success: false, message: `Route not found: ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl}` });
});

// 6. Global 500 Error Handler Middleware
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  res.status(500).json({ success: false, message: 'Internal Server Error', error: err.message });
});

const PORT = process.env.PORT || 5001;
app.listen(PORT, () => console.log(`🚀 BiteOrder API Server running at http://localhost:${PORT}`));

4.2 Defining RESTful API Routes (server/routes/menuRoutes.js)

const express = require('express');
const router = express.Router();
const {
  getMenu,
  getMenuItemById,
  createMenuItem,
  updateMenuItem,
  deleteMenuItem,
} = require('../controllers/menuController');

// Menu Items CRUD Endpoints
router.get('/menu', getMenu);               // GET all dishes (supports ?category=&q=)
router.get('/menu/:id', getMenuItemById);   // GET single dish by ID
router.post('/menu', createMenuItem);       // POST create new dish
router.put('/menu/:id', updateMenuItem);    // PUT update existing dish
router.delete('/menu/:id', deleteMenuItem); // DELETE remove dish

module.exports = router;

4.3 Implementing Controller CRUD Operations & Error Handling (server/controllers/menuController.js)

// 1. GET /api/menu - Retrieve all menu items
exports.getMenu = (req, res) => {
  try {
    const { category, q } = req.query;
    let items = [...menuItems];
    if (category && category !== 'all') {
      items = items.filter(i => i.category.toLowerCase() === category.toLowerCase());
    }
    if (q && q.trim()) {
      items = items.filter(i => i.name.toLowerCase().includes(q.toLowerCase()));
    }
    res.status(200).json({ success: true, count: items.length, data: items });
  } catch (err) {
    res.status(500).json({ success: false, message: 'Server error', error: err.message });
  }
};

// 2. GET /api/menu/:id - Retrieve single menu item by ID (req.params)
exports.getMenuItemById = (req, res) => {
  const itemId = parseInt(req.params.id, 10);
  if (isNaN(itemId)) return res.status(400).json({ success: false, message: 'Invalid ID parameter.' });

  const item = menuItems.find(i => i.id === itemId);
  if (!item) return res.status(404).json({ success: false, message: `Menu item with ID ${itemId} not found.` });

  res.status(200).json({ success: true, data: item });
};

// 3. POST /api/menu - Create new menu item (req.body)
exports.createMenuItem = (req, res) => {
  const { name, category, price, isVeg = true, description } = req.body;
  if (!name || !price) {
    return res.status(400).json({ success: false, message: 'Validation Error: name and price are required.' });
  }

  const newId = menuItems.length > 0 ? Math.max(...menuItems.map(i => i.id)) + 1 : 1;
  const newItem = { id: newId, name, category, price, isVeg, description, rating: 4.5 };
  menuItems.push(newItem);

  res.status(201).json({ success: true, message: 'Menu item created successfully.', data: newItem });
};

// 4. PUT /api/menu/:id - Update existing menu item
exports.updateMenuItem = (req, res) => {
  const itemId = parseInt(req.params.id, 10);
  const index = menuItems.findIndex(i => i.id === itemId);
  if (index === -1) {
    return res.status(404).json({ success: false, message: `Menu item with ID ${itemId} not found. Cannot update.` });
  }

  menuItems[index] = { ...menuItems[index], ...req.body, id: itemId };
  res.status(200).json({ success: true, message: `Menu item with ID ${itemId} updated successfully.`, data: menuItems[index] });
};

// 5. DELETE /api/menu/:id - Remove menu item
exports.deleteMenuItem = (req, res) => {
  const itemId = parseInt(req.params.id, 10);
  const index = menuItems.findIndex(i => i.id === itemId);
  if (index === -1) {
    return res.status(404).json({ success: false, message: `Menu item with ID ${itemId} not found. Cannot delete.` });
  }

  const [deletedItem] = menuItems.splice(index, 1);
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    message: `Menu item "${deletedItem.name}" (ID: ${itemId}) deleted successfully.`,
    deletedData: deletedItem,
  });
};

4.4 Frontend React Client Integration (client/src/pages/MenuPage.jsx)

// Dynamic data fetch from Express REST API
useEffect(() => {
  const fetchMenu = async () => {
    try {
      const res = await fetch('http://localhost:5001/api/menu');
      const json = await res.json();
      if (json.success && Array.isArray(json.data)) {
        setRawMenuItems(json.data);
        setApiStatus('connected');
      }
    } catch (err) {
      console.warn('API offline, using fallback catalog');
    }
  };
  fetchMenu();
}, []);

7. Result

The RESTful APIs for the BiteOrder Restaurant Ordering & Management System were successfully developed using Node.js and Express.js and comprehensively tested using Postman. Complete CRUD operations (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), route parameter parsing (req.params), request payload handling (req.body), HTTP status codes (200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found), and live bidirectional React frontend synchronization were verified and documented.
